Now, here are 4 news stories that broke in the morning to watch out for:
U.S. business activity accelerates to 5-year high in September:

to 58.4 in September from 56.0 in August, marking a 62-month high, according to S&P Global data released Wednesday. The services sector drove growth with output rising at the steepest pace in over five years, while manufacturing output reached its fastest rate since April 2022 at 57.0. S&P Global's Chris Williamson noted the data points to annualized growth of around 5%, though input costs spiked at the steepest rate in four years as fuel and transport expenses surged.
Oil shipping costs surge past $1.2M/day amid Middle East tanker shortage:

a Very Large Crude Carrier between the Middle East and Asia has surpassed $1.2 million per day for the first time, more than doubling since late August, the Financial Times reported. The war in Iran has created a severe shortage of the world's largest tankers as vessels reroute and travel longer distances. Energy Aspects founder Amrita Sen said landed crude costs in Asia have soared toward $150/bbl, while diesel prices have reached $180/bbl in Singapore and over $200/bbl in Europe. Front-month Brent crude rebounded 2.3% to $101.55/bbl on Wednesday after five straight sessions of declines.
U.S. dollar climbs to July highs on Fed rate hike expectations:

The dollar index  rose 0.4% to 101.1, reaching its highest level since July after Federal Reserve officials signaled more rate hikes may be needed to combat inflation. Markets are now pricing a 53% chance of an October rate hike following last week's increase, the Fed's first in three years. Jim Bianco of Bianco Research noted the elevated odds contrast with Wall Street expectations, with the October meeting falling just one week before the U.S. midterm election.
Disney hikes Disney+ and Hulu prices across ad-free plans:

announced price increases across its streaming services, raising ad-free Disney+ Premium by 13% to $21.49 per month. The ad-free Disney+ and Hulu bundle will increase by $2 to $21.99 per month, while ad-supported tiers remain unchanged at $12.99. For comparison, Netflix's similar ad-free plan costs $26.99 per month. According to Bloomberg, subscribers will be notified of the price hikes on Wednesday.
